title: Two what-ifs: an open yuan, and a one-time US debt reset
intro: Both are tested against data and history. China opening fully is unlikely and would help the dollar before hurting it. A one-time US revaluation that clears half the debt fails the arithmetic, and the likeliest path is slow erosion by inflation and captive buyers.

items.q: What if China opens its controls on money flowing in and out, changing the policy that limits the yuan (full capital account convertibility)? What happens to the yuan's role, the dollar, Treasuries, gold and the scenario odds?
a: China runs a deliberately half-open system. Citizens may buy only about $50,000 of foreign currency a year. Foreigners come in through licensed pipes (QFII, Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and since 2025 repo access). Residents go out only through rationed ones: QDII quotas stood at $176.17B at end June 2026 with none issued in the second quarter, and Southbound Bond Connect was raised to 800 billion yuan a year on 2026-07-07. The PBoC sets a daily fixing and has guided the yuan to 6.67, its strongest since 2022. This is the "impossible trinity" choice: Beijing keeps control of its own interest rates and a managed yuan, so it cannot also let money move freely. Full convertibility would mean a floating yuan, giving up the cheap captive deposits that fund state banks and local governments, much deeper open bond markets (foreigners hold only about RMB 3.2T, roughly $480B) and courts that foreign creditors trust.

The one real test went badly. After a small devaluation on 2015-08-11, reserves fell $512.66B in 2015 alone and from about $3.99T in mid 2014 to under $3T by January 2017, while the yuan fell from about 6.11 to 6.95. Beijing re-tightened in 2017. The yuan joined the IMF's SDR basket in 2016, yet it is still only 2.11% of world reserves against the dollar's 56.70%, and 2.4% to 3.1% of SWIFT payments. The 2026 to 2030 plan promises "high-quality" and "autonomous" capital account opening, which in practice means more quotas and pilots, with an analyst target of about 80% of capital items convertible by 2030, not full freedom.

If China did open fully, the first wave would most likely go out, not in. Chinese households hold about RMB 167T of deposits (about $25T) earning little, while the US 10-year pays 5.13%. Moving 5% to 10% of that abroad is $1.25T to $2.5T, or 37% to 74% of China's $3.40T reserves. Expect a weaker yuan, Chinese money buying US, Hong Kong and Singapore assets, the PBoC selling some of its $590.7B of Treasuries, and a stronger dollar. Net Treasury demand would be roughly flat in that phase. Only later, and only if the rules hold, would foreign inflows and index weights build a reserve role for the yuan in yen or pound territory (4% to 6%, perhaps 10% by the 2040s), with the dollar drifting to about 52% to 55%. Chinese household gold buying, partly a substitute for blocked foreign assets, would likely ease, while the PBoC would keep buying gold because a yuan held in China is still freezable by Beijing.

Winners would be Chinese savers and private firms, global asset managers and US asset markets in the outflow phase. Losers would be state banks and local government vehicles that live on captive deposits, Hong Kong's role as the only gate, and in the long run the dollar's reserve share. Odds: full convertibility by 2030 is 3 in 100, by 2035 8, by 2050 25. A large partial step (the $50,000 quota lifted or abolished, or about 80% of items convertible) is 25 by 2030 and 40 by 2035. Signs that would come first: the individual quota raised or made a registration, QDII and Connect quotas abolished rather than topped up, the 2% daily band widened, free-trade-account rules extended nationwide, legal protections for foreign creditors, and Chinese yields converging with US yields.

Scenario odds do not change today, because the event is unlikely and its effects come years later. If full convertibility were announced, the desk would move H0 from 62/15/1/22 to 62/14/1/23 (a 2015-style yuan episode adds stress), H1 from 44/23/3/30 to 40/27/3/30 and H2 from 31/28/10/31 to 26/33/10/31, because a convertible yuan would be the first credible rival reserve asset. The desk's S2 is defined as gold and neutral assets, so that shift would need an "S2b multipolar" label.

v.g: For Beijing, full opening means losing the captive deposits that fund state banks, local governments and industrial policy, and accepting outside judgment of its currency and courts. It has chosen control every time the trade-off was sharp, so expect quotas and pilots, not a big bang. For Washington, a sudden opening would first push Chinese savings into US assets.
v.b: Treat China's opening as quota news, not regime change. Watch the $50,000 quota, QDII and Southbound Connect quotas, the daily band and the fixing. A real opening would first mean a weaker yuan and a wave of Chinese buying abroad, and later bigger index weights for Chinese bonds.
v.p: Nothing here changes the dollar in your pocket soon. If China opened, the first thing you might notice is Chinese money chasing homes, stocks and bonds abroad, and cheaper Chinese goods if the yuan fell. Holding yuan as easily as euros is a 2040s question at the earliest.

items.q: What if the Putin adviser's claim (Anton Kobyakov, 2025-09-06: when part of the US national debt is placed in stablecoins, the authorities will devalue this debt) is one form of a real possibility: the US getting out of its debt by revaluation, one time, clearing 50% to 80% of it and starting a new currency yardstick? Is that the closest probable path among those discussed?
a: No. A one-time clearance is the least probable path, and the most probable one is the quiet version of what Kobyakov described: slow erosion by inflation while captive buyers, now including stablecoins, hold part of the debt at low yields. "Revaluation" can mean five things for a dollar debtor: marking up gold, devaluing the dollar against gold or other currencies, inflation above the interest paid, swapping into a new unit (Germany's Rentenmark in 1923, Brazil's real in 1994) or an explicit haircut (Argentina 2005, about 75% to 77% lost in present value). Only the haircut clears 50% to 80% at once, and for the issuer of the world's collateral that is a default.

The arithmetic rules out the gold route. The US holds 261.5M ounces booked at $42.2222. To clear 50% of the $32.57T debt held by the public, gold would have to be revalued to about $62,300 an ounce, and to about $99,700 for 80%, 15 to 24 times today's $4,078. The gain would arrive as $16T to $26T of new central bank money, three to five times today's base money. If the Fed pays interest on it, nothing is saved. If it does not, banks are taxed and prices rise. Either way the one-time event turns into inflation. Devaluing the dollar against other currencies does not cut a debt owed in dollars at all.

Inflation alone is weaker than it looks. Halving the real debt needs about 15% a year for 5 years or 7% for 10, and only if nothing were ever refinanced. But bills are 22% of the debt, average maturity is 71 months and the primary deficit is about 2.9% of GDP. In this lane's model even 10 years of 20% inflation takes the debt ratio from 100% to only about 84% unless the Fed caps yields. The best US precedent, 1946 to 1974, cut about 80 points of GDP over 28 years: about 30 from primary surpluses and about 40 from capped rates and surprise inflation (Acalin and Ball, 2026). The UK cut 206 points over 27 years under exchange controls. Japan expects about 14 points by 2031. The burden would fall mostly on Americans: foreigners hold 28.6% of debt held by the public and 23% of gross debt, while Social Security benefits, tax brackets and $2.17T of TIPS rise with prices.

Kobyakov's stablecoin channel is real only in its small part. Holders earn zero by law and many are foreign, so if real rates go negative they carry part of the loss. But the tokens hold bills of 93 days or less, the debt that reprices fastest, the Treasury still pays the market rate to the issuer, and stablecoins are about 0.9% of the debt. At $2T of supply and a 2-point inflation gap the transfer would be about $40B a year, about 0.1% of GDP. Grade: half-right on capture, a D3 as a devaluation plan.

Verdict by probability. One-time clearance of 50% to 80% by revaluation by 2035: 1 in 100. Inflation erasing at least 20% of today's debt's purchasing power by 2035 (average inflation of about 2.5% or more): 55. The strict version, 20% to 40% erased after interest (real yields of minus 2.4% to minus 5.4% a year for nine years): 10. A new US unit of account replacing the dollar by 2040: 2. A new international yardstick at accord level by 2040: 12. The closest probable path is gradual erosion plus financial repression lite, which erases about a fifth of the debt's real value by 2035 but does not shrink the debt ratio unless deficits also fall. Tells: a 10-year breakeven above 2.75%, Fed long-end buying or yield language, stablecoins above 10% of bills after 2027-01-18, a cut in the TIPS share of issuance, and any change to the $42.2222 gold book value.

v.g: The choice is not reset or no reset but how visible the loss is and who carries it. A one-time revaluation is the most visible and least effective tool. Inflation above coupons plus captive buyers is the least visible and is already partly built. The binding limits are the bond market, indexed spending and a Fed that is hiking.
v.b: Price the slow path. It rewards owners of real assets, pricing power and fixed-rate debt, and punishes long nominal lenders. A gold revaluation would be a headline, not a balance-sheet event, unless it came with yield caps.
v.p: Nobody will wake up to a new dollar with half the debt gone. The realistic risk is a decade in which prices rise faster than the interest on your savings. Indexed income and owned real assets protect you. Cash and stablecoins do not, because they pay you little or nothing while prices rise.
